meta.title: The Monday-Morning Test
meta.subtitle: Turning shop-floor reality into same-day operating action across 120 APAC stores

slides.title: The Monday-Morning Test
slides.subtitle: A joined-up proposal for seeing, hearing, bottling, and scaling what works in store
slides.script: We are starting with the test that matters operationally: what we know on Monday morning. Today, Monday tells us what happened last week, after the customer conversations, manager decisions, missed opportunities, and roster work have already passed. Our proposal changes that rhythm. We connect Spacesight, Echo, Harbor Wiki, and Alivia so RetailCo can see what is happening on the floor, hear what staff are saying, bottle the best behaviours, and turn one real store into a practical proposal before we talk about scaling.

slides.title: RetailCo's operating scale makes delay expensive

metrics.label: gap between best and worst managers

slides.script: We are not looking at a small visibility problem. We are looking at 120 stores, 2,000 frontline staff, and a three-times performance gap between the best and worst store managers. At that scale, even simple questions become hard when the answer arrives in a spreadsheet after the week is over. We do not need to start by boiling the ocean. We need to prove, in one store, that the operating facts can move closer to the operating moment, and then use that proof to guide the broader conversation.

slides.title: What Monday knows today versus what Monday could know

rows.right: Same-day floor signals from Spacesight
Scored frontline conversations from Echo
Repeatable playbooks in Harbor Wiki
Roster workflow scoped as an open item

slides.script: We are reframing the proposal around the Monday-morning difference. Today, Monday is backward-looking: a spreadsheet, anecdotes, and manager instinct. Under this proposal, Monday becomes diagnostic. Spacesight shows what happened on the floor. Echo shows what staff actually said to customers. Harbor Wiki turns the patterns from strong managers into a searchable operating playbook. Scheduling is different: none of these products is a rostering engine, so we should not pretend it is solved. We can, however, scope the coordination pain clearly as part of the proposal.

slides.title: Fix fastest where the signal already exists

rows.right: Spacesight captures what is happening in store.
Echo captures and scores what staff say.
Harbor Wiki turns winning behaviours into answers.
Alivia packages the pilot evidence into a client proposal.

slides.script: We would order the work by what can be fixed fastest. The fastest signal is the signal already happening every day: movement on the floor and conversations with customers. Spacesight and Echo capture that reality without waiting for a Monday spreadsheet. Once we can see and hear the operation, Harbor Wiki gives us a place to bottle the behaviours that work. Alivia then turns the evidence into a structured proposal, so the next discussion is not abstract transformation. It is a concrete view of what one store showed us.

slides.quote: I have no idea what actually happens on my shop floor. I get a spreadsheet on Monday about last week.
slides.script: We heard this as the core operating frustration. It is not that RetailCo lacks data; it is that the data arrives too late and too far away from the shop floor. By Monday, the team can explain last week, but they cannot change last week. Spacesight directly addresses that gap by showing what is happening in store. Echo complements it by adding the customer conversation layer. Together, they turn the shop floor from a blind spot into an observable system that management can discuss while the facts are still fresh.

slides.title: From observed reality to Monday action

steps.label: See
steps.text: Spacesight identifies floor patterns as they happen.

steps.label: Hear
steps.text: Echo captures real frontline customer conversations.

steps.label: Compare
steps.text: Strong and weak moments become visible side by side.

steps.label: Act
steps.text: Managers coach from evidence, not memory.

slides.script: We are proposing a simple operating loop. First, we see the floor through Spacesight. Then, we hear the staff and customer interaction through Echo. Once those two signals sit together, RetailCo can compare what high-performing moments look like against weaker ones. That matters because coaching becomes specific. We are no longer asking a manager to remember what happened, defend an anecdote, or wait for a weekly report. We are giving the store team evidence they can use to adjust behaviour while the week is still unfolding.

slides.title: Bottle the 3x manager gap

rows.right: Echo and Spacesight reveal the repeatable behaviours.
Harbor Wiki converts it into a searchable playbook.
The answer is available without waiting for coaching.
Alivia packages what to scale after the pilot.

slides.script: The three-times gap between best and worst store managers is the biggest clue that RetailCo already has answers inside the business. The issue is that those answers are trapped in people, habits, and local context. We would use Spacesight and Echo to identify what the best managers do differently, then use Harbor Wiki to make those behaviours searchable and reusable. The goal is not to replace managerial judgement. It is to give every manager access to the moves that already work inside RetailCo.

slides.title: Make onboarding depend on the playbook, not the shift

cards.heading: Capture
cards.body: Spacesight and Echo identify real examples from the floor and conversations.

cards.heading: Convert
cards.body: Harbor Wiki turns those examples into simple, searchable guidance.

cards.heading: Coach
cards.body: New hires learn from proven RetailCo behaviours, not whoever is nearby.

slides.script: The six-week onboarding pain is closely related to the manager gap. If a new hire learns only from whoever happens to be working that day, quality will vary by store, shift, and luck. We would change the dependency. Real examples from Spacesight and Echo become the raw material. Harbor Wiki turns those examples into guidance that new hires can search and managers can reinforce. That means onboarding can still feel local and practical, but the core behaviours come from RetailCo’s best observed practice rather than informal handover.

slides.title: Be honest about scheduling

rows.right: No listed product is a workforce scheduling engine.
Alivia can document the pain inside the proposal.
We can map who coordinates, when, and why.
Treat scheduling as an adjacent workstream, not a hidden claim.

slides.script: We should call out scheduling plainly. RetailCo told us that getting one roster set takes coordination across many people and teams. Spacesight, Echo, and Harbor Wiki do not become a rostering platform just because scheduling is painful. So our proposal should separate what we can solve now from what we should scope next. Alivia can capture the scheduling workflow and include it as an adjacent workstream in the proposal. That gives RetailCo a clear decision: prove the floor intelligence loop first, while documenting the roster problem properly.

slides.title: Use one real store to build the proposal

rows.right: Floor visibility section
Conversation quality section
Harbor Wiki playbook section
Open workstream section

slides.script: We recommend building the proposal from one real store rather than from assumptions. In that store, Spacesight gives us floor evidence, Echo gives us conversation evidence, and Harbor Wiki shows how the best behaviours can be converted into reusable guidance. Alivia then assembles the case back to RetailCo in a format that is grounded in actual store reality. Scheduling stays visible in that output as an open workstream. This keeps the proposal practical: what we proved, what we can scale, and what still needs a dedicated solution.

slides.text: The proposal is not another report; it is a feedback loop from floor reality to manager playbook.
slides.kicker: See it. Hear it. Bottle it. Propose it.
slides.script: We want this to feel different from another analytics report. The value is the loop. Spacesight sees the floor. Echo hears the conversation. Harbor Wiki bottles the behaviours that explain stronger performance. Alivia turns that evidence into a proposal RetailCo can actually evaluate. That loop directly answers three of the four pains: Monday visibility, the three-times manager gap, and inconsistent six-week onboarding. The fourth pain, scheduling, is not swept away. It is carried forward honestly as an adjacent workstream with evidence from the pilot.

slides.title: Our ask: test this in one real store
slides.subtitle: Prove the Monday-morning difference before scaling the conversation.
bullets: Run Spacesight, Echo, and Harbor Wiki around real workflows
Use Alivia to produce the scale proposal
Review scheduling as a documented adjacent workstream
slides.script: Our ask is deliberately small and concrete. Let us run this against one real store before we scale the conversation across 120. We would use that store to test the Monday-morning difference: what RetailCo can see, what it can hear, what it can bottle, and what still needs a separate scheduling answer. Then Alivia turns the findings into the proposal for the next decision. If the pilot does not make the operating reality clearer, we should learn that early. If it does, we have a grounded path to discuss scale.

approach.angle: Lead with the Monday-morning test: what the COO knows on Monday today, versus what they would know under this proposal.
approach.device: Structure around the things the customer said, but re-ordered by what you can fix fastest.
approach.opener: Open on the numbers of their operation, so the scale of the problem lands first.
approach.close: Close by asking to run the proposal against one real store before scaling the conversation.
